cues.text: Welcome to Equilibrium.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Equilibrium is dynamic: opposing changes continue at equal, nonzero rates.
Imagine liquid water in a closed container at fixed temperature.
Water evaporates while vapour condenses.
At equilibrium the amounts remain constant because the two rates balance, not
because the molecules stop moving.
Equal rates do not require equal amounts.
Similar reasoning applies to melting and freezing, sublimation and deposition,
and reversible chemical reactions.
The conditions and phases must be specified.
For a gas dissolved in a liquid, one common Henry law convention is gas
partial
pressure equals Henry's constant times the dissolved gas mole fraction.
At fixed temperature and pressure, a larger constant in this convention means
a
smaller dissolved mole fraction.
Suppose the gas partial pressure is two bar and the constant is one thousand
bar.
Divide two by one thousand to obtain mole fraction zero point zero zero two.
Doubling the partial pressure doubles that mole fraction within the dilute
model.
A different convention can put the concentration on the other side, so do not
compare constants before checking definitions.
This distinction between a changing rate and a fixed equilibrium composition
will guide the remaining chapters.
The reaction quotient Q describes the present mixture.
The equilibrium constant K describes equilibrium at the specified temperature.
For a balanced reaction, multiply product activities raised to their
coefficients and divide by the corresponding reactant product.
Pure solids and pure liquids have unit activity in their reference states and
are omitted from the usual expression.
If Q is smaller than K, the forward direction is favoured; if larger, the
reverse direction is favoured.
Consider hydrogen plus iodine forming two hydrogen iodide molecules, all
gases.
In the ideal concentration convention, Q is hydrogen iodide concentration
squared divided by hydrogen concentration times iodine concentration.
Let those concentrations be zero point two zero, zero point one zero, and zero
point one zero molar respectively.
Q is four.
If K is fifty at that temperature, the mixture proceeds forward.
Reversing a reaction replaces K with its reciprocal.
Doubling every coefficient squares K.
For conventional ideal gas expressions, K p equals K c times R T raised to
the gaseous mole change.
In this example, two gas molecules replace two gas molecules, so the exponent
is zero.
Keep the pressure, concentration and gas constant conventions consistent.
Rigorous thermodynamic equilibrium constants are dimensionless and use
activities relative to reference states.
Le Chatelier's principle helps predict a response, but checking Q is more
reliable than memorizing slogans.
For nitrogen plus three hydrogen forming two ammonia molecules, compression at
unchanged temperature increases all reacting ideal gas partial pressures.
The denominator in Q has total power four, while the numerator has power two.
If all partial pressures double, Q falls by a factor of four.
Starting at equilibrium, Q is then below K, so formation of ammonia is
favoured.
Compression does not change K at fixed temperature.
Adding an inert ideal gas at fixed volume leaves the reacting gases' partial
pressures unchanged, so it causes no shift in this model.
At fixed total pressure the volume increases, and the outcome can differ.
Heating changes K and favours the endothermic direction.
For an exothermic forward reaction, heating favours the reverse direction.
A catalyst accelerates the approach to equilibrium without changing its
composition or K at the same temperature.
Removing a product can favour further product formation, provided the relevant
phase and activity actually change.
Adding more of a pure solid already present does not simply multiply its
activity.
State the temperature, volume or pressure constraint.
An acid can be described in several ways.
An Arrhenius acid increases hydrogen ion concentration in water.
A Bronsted acid donates a proton, and a Bronsted base accepts one.
A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair.
A conjugate acid and base differ by one proton.
Ammonia and ammonium are one such pair.
Acid strength refers to ionization behaviour, while concentration describes
how
much acid is present.
Do not infer pH from the word strong alone.
Strictly, pH is minus the base ten logarithm of hydrogen ion activity.
In an elementary dilute model we use the numerical molar concentration.
At twenty five degrees Celsius, the water ion product is approximately ten to
the minus fourteen.
The sum of pH and pOH is then approximately fourteen.
A hydrogen ion concentration of ten to the minus three molar gives pH three.
A hydroxide concentration of ten to the minus five molar gives pOH five and pH
nine at this temperature.
Neutrality means equal hydrogen and hydroxide activities, not an unconditional
pH of seven at every temperature.
Extremely dilute acid solutions require water ionization to be included; a
strong acid concentration of ten to the minus eight molar cannot simply be
assigned pH eight.
For a monoprotic weak acid, let the initial concentration be C and the
dissociated amount be x.
Ignoring water ionization, the acid constant equals x squared divided by C
minus x.
If x is much smaller than C, replacing the denominator by C gives x
approximately the square root of the acid constant times C.
With C equal to zero point one zero zero molar and the acid constant ten to
the
minus five, x is approximately zero point zero zero one zero zero molar.
The pH is about three, and only one percent dissociates.
That small fraction supports the approximation.
Now take both C and the acid constant as zero point zero zero one zero zero.
The shortcut predicts complete dissociation, contradicting its own assumption.
Solve the quadratic instead.
The positive root is minus the acid constant plus the square root of its
square
plus four times the acid constant times C, all divided by two.
The result is about zero point zero zero zero six one eight molar, giving pH
three point two zero nine.
About sixty two percent dissociates.
The example shows why weak does not automatically mean slightly dissociated at
every dilution.
Check both the neglected dissociation fraction and whether water's own ions
matter.
A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base in useful amounts.
The acid consumes added base, while the conjugate base consumes added acid.
First complete the strong acid or base reaction using moles.
Only then apply the Henderson Hasselbalch approximation: pH equals p K a plus
the base ten logarithm of remaining conjugate base divided by remaining acid.
Suppose the buffer contains twenty millimoles of acid and thirty millimoles of
conjugate base.
Add five millimoles of strong acid.
It consumes five millimoles of conjugate base and forms five millimoles of
weak
acid, leaving twenty five millimoles of each.
Their concentration ratio equals their mole ratio because they share the same
final volume.
The ratio is one, so with p K a four point seven six, the final pH is
approximately four point seven six.
Using the original thirty over twenty ratio would ignore the neutralization.
A ten to one base to acid ratio would instead add one pH unit.
Diluting both partners equally initially preserves their ratio approximately,
but reduces buffer capacity.
If one partner is exhausted, stop using the two partner buffer formula and
account for excess strong reagent and any relevant hydrolysis.
Salt solutions need not be neutral.
Acetate accepts a proton from water and produces hydroxide, so sodium acetate
is basic in the elementary aqueous model.
Ammonium can donate a proton to water, so ammonium chloride is acidic.
Sodium and chloride are spectators here.
For a conjugate pair at a given temperature, the acid constant times the base
constant equals the water ion product.
Consider zero point one zero zero molar sodium acetate at twenty five degrees
Celsius.
If the acetic acid constant is ten to the minus five, acetate's base constant
is ten to the minus nine.
The small hydrolysis estimate gives hydroxide concentration equal to the
square
root of the base constant times concentration, or ten to the minus five molar.
The pOH is five and the pH is nine.
Only zero point zero one percent of the acetate hydrolyses, so replacing its
remaining concentration by the starting value is justified.
The hydroxide concentration is also large compared with the neutral water
background in this example.
A salt of a strong acid and strong base is approximately neutral when neither
ion hydrolyses appreciably.
Salts with two reacting ions, amphiprotic species and very dilute solutions
need additional equilibrium analysis.
Identify the reacting ion before choosing a shortcut.
Solubility products depend on stoichiometry.
Silver chloride produces one silver ion and one chloride ion, so its dilute
ion
product is their concentration product.
In pure water, molar solubility s gives a product of s squared.
If an illustrative solubility product is ten to the minus ten, the solubility
is ten to the minus five molar.
With zero point zero one zero molar background chloride and no competing
reactions, the approximate solubility falls to ten to the minus eight molar.
Check that this is small compared with the background.
A salt producing one A ion and two B ions instead gives four times s cubed.
Mixing requires dilution before comparing the ion product with the solubility
product.
Mix equal volumes of silver and chloride stock solutions, each two times ten
to
the minus five molar.
Each concentration halves, so the initial ion product is ten to the minus ten.
With the illustrative constant above, this is exactly the saturation boundary,
not supersaturation.
A larger ion product permits precipitation; a smaller one permits more
dissolution if solid is available.
Common ions usually reduce solubility, but complex formation and acid base
reactions can modify the result.
Use the seven worked examples and twelve original questions in the notes to
practise these checks.
Pressure and concentration equilibrium expressions must use compatible
conventions.
For an ideal gas, partial pressure equals concentration times R T.
If the pressure quotient uses each pressure divided by its standard pressure
and the concentration quotient uses each concentration divided by its standard
concentration, their conversion includes R T times standard concentration
divided by standard pressure.
Raise that dimensionless factor to the gaseous product mole count minus the
gaseous reactant mole count.
For dinitrogen tetroxide forming two nitrogen dioxide molecules, the change is
one.
Take standard concentration one mole per litre, standard pressure one bar,
temperature three hundred kelvin and R zero point zero eight three one four
litre bar per mole kelvin.
The conversion factor is twenty four point nine four two.
A supplied concentration based constant of zero point one zero zero therefore
corresponds to a pressure based constant about two point four nine four under
these conventions.
When the gaseous mole change is zero, the factor cancels.
Count gaseous species only and state the standards rather than silently
combining incompatible units or treating every reported constant as the same
numerical quantity.
Gas dissociation changes the total number of molecules, so the reacted
fraction
is not generally the same as the product mole fraction.
Begin with one mole of pure dinitrogen tetroxide.
If a fraction alpha dissociates, one minus alpha mole remains and two alpha
moles of nitrogen dioxide form.
The total is one plus alpha.
At twenty percent dissociation, the amounts are zero point eight and zero
point
four mole, with a total of one point two.
The nitrogen dioxide mole fraction is therefore one third and the tetroxide
fraction two thirds.
At total pressure one bar, their partial pressures are one third bar and two
thirds bar.
With standard pressure one bar, the dimensionless pressure quotient is the
square of one third divided by two thirds, giving one sixth.
The general expression contains four alpha squared divided by one minus alpha
squared, multiplied by total pressure divided by standard pressure.
Check both atom balance and total moles before inserting a pressure.
This model starts with pure reactant and assumes ideal gases without an inert
gas or another competing reaction.
In a strong acid strong base titration, calculate the neutralization amounts
before the remaining ion concentration.
Start with twenty five millilitres of zero point one zero zero molar
hydrochloric acid.
It contains zero point zero zero two five zero mole of acid.
Adding twenty millilitres of equally concentrated sodium hydroxide consumes
zero point zero zero two zero zero mole, leaving zero point zero zero zero
five
zero mole of hydrogen ions in forty five millilitres.
The concentration is about zero point zero one one one molar and p H about one
point nine five.
At twenty five millilitres of base, the stoichiometric amounts are equal.
For this ideal strong acid strong base example at twenty five degrees Celsius,
p H is approximately seven.
At thirty millilitres, excess hydroxide is zero point zero zero zero five zero
mole in fifty five millilitres, giving p O H about two point zero four and p H
about eleven point nine six.
Total volume matters on both sides of equivalence.
A weak acid titration has different equilibrium behaviour, so do not transfer
the neutral equivalence conclusion to every acid base pair.
A solubility product constrains free ion activities, not the total amount of
every metal containing species in solution.
For a simple dilute silver chloride model, use the concentration product as an
approximation to the activity expression.
With illustrative solubility product one point eight times ten to the minus
ten, pure water gives equal silver and chloride concentrations and a molar
solubility about one point three four times ten to the minus five.
Now suppose the solution already contains zero point zero one zero molar
chloride.
If additional dissolution is small, free chloride remains approximately that
value.
Divide the solubility product by zero point zero one zero to obtain silver
concentration one point eight times ten to the minus eight molar.
The added dissolution is tiny relative to the initial chloride, so the
approximation is self consistent.
This common ion lowers simple solubility in the stated model.
Complex formation, other equilibria and nonideal activities can alter the
result.
In particular, total dissolved silver need not equal free silver when
complexes
are important.
Check what concentration the question actually asks for before applying the
product expression.
An amphiprotic species can accept or donate a proton.
Hydrogen carbonate is a familiar intermediate in a diprotic acid system.
Its acid behaviour is controlled by the second acid dissociation constant,
while its base behaviour is related to the first constant through the water
ion
product.
Under the appropriate intermediate salt approximation, p H is approximately
half the sum of the two p K a values.
For illustrative values six point three and ten point three, the estimate is
eight point three.
This is a mildly basic result even though the formula contains hydrogen.
Do not classify a salt as acidic simply because its anion still carries a
proton.
The average formula assumes conditions where the amphiprotic salt contribution
dominates water effects and the approximations used in its derivation are
adequate.
Very dilute solutions, additional acids or bases, and important competing
equilibria can require a fuller mass and charge balance.
The two constants must refer to the same acid system, solvent and temperature.
A useful answer states the model and its limits alongside the numerical
average.
